_comment: Presentation. ALL of it is TUNABLE and none of it is a mechanic. The expected feedback is 'too dark', 'the grass is the wrong green', 'the creatures don't move enough' — every one of those has to be answerable by editing this file rather than by editing a scene.
_comment_scale: Nothing here sets a collider or a hit range. Art is fitted to the gameplay size the species and the controller already declare; if a value in this file could change how far an attack reaches, it is in the wrong file.

trainer._comment_height: Metres, matched to the CharacterBody3D capsule in scenes/player/player.tscn. The model is measured and scaled to this, so a replacement of any size drops in without touching the scene.
trainer._comment_yaw: Degrees of correction for which way the source model faces. Verified from a survey frame, not assumed — there is no convention across asset packs.
trainer._comment_clips: Clip names as they exist in the .glb. Kenney's Blocky Characters ship 27; these are the six the game currently drives. A replacement model with different names is a data edit here.
trainer._comment_libraries: KayKit ships characters and animations separately: Ranger.glb has the mesh and a 23-bone rig but zero clips, and the clips live in shared libraries built on the same rig. These are merged into the character's AnimationPlayer at load. Getting this wrong is a trainer frozen in a T-pose.
trainer._comment_model: Styloo 'The Company' knight (CC0). Replaces the KayKit Ranger, whom the critic measured as a Mii: skin pixels outnumbering clothing 1.36:1, 2.01:1 and 4.50:1 across three frames, because the survey sees him from behind and he is a bald flesh-coloured egg — 'in 05 the character is, numerically, mostly a floating head'. Its verdict was that the trainer alone decides the Palworld read before anything else in the frame is considered. This one is armoured, proportioned, and 2K-textured.
trainer._comment_retarget: The knight ships ZERO clips on a 216-bone Rigify skeleton that shares no bone names with the 23-bone KayKit rig the 25 clips are authored on. `animation_retarget.gd` replays them across using the map below. Rotation only, as a delta from each rig's own rest pose — copying raw rotations puts the arms at whatever angle the OTHER rig rests at, which is wrong by a constant in every clip.
trainer._comment_hide_bones: Bones whose vertices should not be drawn. `DEF-shield` and the unparented `DEF-bone.01` chain carry a shield and a sword modelled into the same skinned mesh as the body; no clip drives them, so they hang in bind pose beside the trainer. They would have to go even if they sat correctly on his back: the human cannot fight, so arming him promises the wrong game.
trainer._comment_retarget_bones: SOURCE bone : TARGET bone, and every entry on both sides was read off the two skeletons rather than assumed. The first draft of this map was written from the Rigify convention and had three bones the KayKit rig does not own (`upperchest`, `neck`, `shoulder.l/r`) and one the knight does not (`root`, whose root is `DEF-spine`). Bones absent from EITHER side are left out rather than mapped hopefully: `unmapped()` reports them, and a mapping that names a bone nobody has is a limb missing from all twenty-five clips at once.
trainer._comment_retarget_chain: The rigs disagree about how many bones a spine is. Ours is hips-spine-chest-head; Rigify's is DEF-spine through .006 with the neck at .004/.005. Each of ours goes to the target bone that does the same STRUCTURAL job — `chest` to `DEF-spine.003` because that is where Rigify hangs the shoulders, which is what our chest is for. The unmapped links in between hold their rest pose, so the neck stays straight rather than being driven by a bone that does not exist.
trainer._comment_align_rest: SOURCE bone names whose two rest poses are different POSES rather than different conventions. Measured, not guessed: with the delta transfer correct, every mapped bone's animated direction sits a CONSTANT angle from the source's at every frame of the cycle, and that constant is its rest difference — 0.6° at the chest, 5.1° at the thighs, 14.5° at the pelvis, and 52–60° down the whole arm. The arm figure is the T-pose the KayKit rig rests in against the 52° A-pose the knight rests in, so every clip's arm track spends ~78° lowering an arm that is already lowered, and his hands ended up crossed in front of his groin. Bones listed here are AIMED BY THE CLIP instead. The spine is deliberately absent: its 14.5° is Rigify curving a back that KayKit stacks straight, which is the knight's build and what his mesh is skinned around — flattening it to match would be trading a real difference for a fake one. The legs are absent because 5° is nothing.

sky._comment: Mid-morning, high summer, clear. Taken from the key art board rather than invented: a warm low-contrast sky over saturated grass is most of what makes the reference read as inviting rather than as a tech demo.
sky._comment_panorama: An HDRI panorama, when the time of day names one. The procedural gradient below is the FALLBACK and stays because a missing texture should degrade to the old sky rather than to a black void. The critic measured the procedural sky's horizontal variation at 0.020 against Palworld's 0.140-0.289 and said the build sky 'contributes nothing' — a ProceduralSkyMaterial can make a vertical gradient and a soft sun blob and nothing else, ever. No amount of tuning puts a cloud in it.

sun._comment: One directional light. `pitch` well above the horizon so shadows are short and readable under a top-down-ish combat camera; long raking shadows look dramatic in a screenshot and hide the opponent in a fight.
sun._comment_shadow_fade: Fraction of `shadow_max_distance` at which shadows start dissolving, and whether cascade splits are blended. Both exist to kill the same artefact: the critic found 'a hard shadow-distance cutoff as a horizontal line across 04'. Raising the distance alone only moves the line and costs resolution everywhere nearer, so the distance moved a little and the EDGE became a gradient.
sun._comment_shadow: Normal bias fights the acne that a heightmap terrain produces at grazing angles. Raise it if the ground looks striped; lower it if small props stop casting.
sun._comment_energy: Bright. The first pass at real lighting overshot into gloom: the arena went near-black and the creatures stopped being readable, which is a worse failure than the flat lighting it replaced. Value RANGE was the goal — bright sun, real shadows — not darkness.

environment._comment: Tonemap and fog. ACES holds highlights on sunlit grass instead of clipping them to white, which was the single worst thing about the previous prototype's look.
environment._comment_fog: Very light, and warm rather than grey. It exists to separate near hills from far ones; at any strength where you notice it as fog, it is too strong.
environment._comment_fog_measured: Halved from 0.0022. At the old density the blind critic measured `03-rise-overlook` at mean saturation 0.235 against 0.51 for a frame in the same biome, and said fog was 'eating the world rather than describing depth' — every object past ~150m a grey stamp. The reference does the same job with comparable haze and keeps a saturated tree band in front of it, so the fix is less fog, not less distance.
environment._comment_ambient: Sky ambient with a real colour underneath it. `sky_contribution` blends between the two. Quadrupling ambient energy with pure sky ambient moved the survey frames by NOTHING — sky radiance does not reach the terrain under the Compatibility renderer the harness is forced to use — while an explicit colour lifted the shaded ground by 55%. Specifying both means shaded ground is filled under either renderer, and 'shadows are filled by this much of this colour' is a decision somebody made rather than a side effect of a procedural sky.
environment._comment_fog_round4: Halved again, from 0.0011. frame_stats puts `03-rise-overlook` at chroma 10.7% against the references' 31-74% — the one frame that looks furthest is the one with almost no colour left in it. That is the same finding as round 3, which means the previous halving did not go far enough. Aerial perspective is cut with it, because the two compound and tuning one while leaving the other is how the last round under-shot.
environment._comment_ambient_round4: Raised from 1.25 alongside the ground tint and colour map. Those two decide the albedo; this decides how much light reaches the parts of it the sun does not, which under a -52 degree sun is most of the near field.
environment._comment_exposure_round4: Raised from 1.05. With the tint and colour map near white there is no multiply headroom left, and the photographic albedo's own value of 0.52 is then the floor: 0.52 x 0.84 is a 0.44 diffuse albedo rendering at 0.33, so the shortfall against Palworld's 0.45 median is a LIGHTING one, not an albedo one. Exposure is the lever that says so.
environment._comment_fog_colour_round4: Darkened and pulled green. Raising exposure lifts the distance as well as the near field, and the distance is already the bright end — it measures 0.62 against the near field's 0.33 because fog is painting it with a 0.82-value grey. A darker fog colour keeps the exposure gain in the foreground where the deficit is.

_comment_times: Named hours. Each states ONLY what it changes; everything else comes from the blocks above.
_comment_times_why: The previous survey shipped a frame called `05-spawn-low-sun` whose sky was BIT-IDENTICAL to the midday frame beside it — 46.8% of the image pixel-for-pixel the same — because dropping the sun meant rotating a DirectionalLight3D and nothing else. The sun disc, sky gradient, horizon haze and fog all stayed at noon. The key art board asks for 'day and night create different moods'; a sky that does not move with the sun cannot give one. So the hour is one value and everything derives from it. Nothing should reach for the Sun node directly again.

day._comment: Mid-morning, high summer, clear. The default, and what the biome is designed around.

golden._comment: Late afternoon. Long shadows, warm key, the sky's blue pushed down and the horizon lifted to amber. This is the mood the key art's own sunset panel is selling, and it is the one hour where the meadow gets its warm end of the palette for free.

_comment_creature_motion_removed: The procedural bob that used to be configured here is gone. The creatures are rigged and animated now, so they have real idle, walk, run, attack and death clips — faking motion on top of that would fight the animation.

creatures._comment:
What colour each creature is, per material, applied by scripts/pals/pal_body.gd at load. The same idea data/config/vegetation.json uses on foliage and for the same reason: the Quaternius animal pack ships NO TEXTURES AT ALL — every model is four to eight flat named material zones (`Main`, `Main_Light`, `Hooves`, `Eyes_Black`) — so a material name is a stable handle and a hue is one line. A model can be swapped for another in the same pack and the palette survives.

Applied as a per-instance surface override, never by mutating the shared Mesh, so two creatures of one species cannot end up sharing a repaint and the imported .gltf on disk is never touched.

Keyed by SPECIES rather than globally by material name, which vegetation.json can get away with and this cannot: two models in this pack use the name `Material.001` for two unrelated zones — black fur on the Husky, dark brown hide on the Stag — so a global map would repaint one of them wrong.
creatures._comment_why:
This block exists because of two specific defects the sourcing pass found, both of them MA-02's finding returning — 'saturation 0.12... a grey rock standing on olive ground... your own pal is the least readable object in your own fight':

  Wolf `Main` ships #777972 — pale grey, saturation 0.03, at almost exactly the meadow's own value.
  Frog `Green` ships #80a960 — green, on green.

Neither is fixable by lighting and neither is a bug in the pack: these are naturalistic animal colours, and this game is not naturalistic. The whole roster is repainted rather than only those two, because a palette is a relationship — a fixed wolf standing next to five unfixed pack-default browns is still a frame of browns.

Every hue below is chosen against the meadow's ground AS MEASURED IN A REAL FRAME (`shots/combat/02-arena-opens.png`, eight samples): hue 74–81°, saturation 0.62–0.81, value 0.49–0.67. That is a much brighter and much more saturated green than the olive this block was first written against, because the ground is another milestone's live work and it moved underneath this one — which is the reason the numbers are sampled rather than remembered. Nothing below sits within 30° of hue 77° unless it clears the ground by value instead; every creature separates from it by hue, by value or by both, and no two creatures in the roster share a hue family except the Duskpup and the Gloamfang, which are one creature at two ages.

ALL OF IT IS TUNABLE. None of it is a mechanic.

starter_ground._comment:
Your partner, and therefore the one thing that must never be lost in a frame — the loudest colour in the roster, deliberately.

THIS WAS MEASURED IN A REAL GAME FRAME AND CORRECTED. The first pass set `Main` to #e0873a (saturation 0.74) and `Main_Light` to a cream #f6e3c2, which looked right on a preview stage and rendered in `shots/combat/02-arena-opens.png` at saturation 0.23-0.40 — a pale cream animal, less readable than the Meadow Hopper it was fighting, which is MA-02's exact finding about the pal you own. Two things did it: the meadow's ACES exposure lifts everything by a lot, and the fleece the cream was on is most of the alpaca's visible area. So the source colours are now deep enough that what comes OUT the far end of the tonemapper is orange.

wild_rabbit._comment: The practice creature, thrown at twenty times, and small enough to lose in grass. Bright gold at value 0.95 reads instantly against dark green — the exact colour and the exact reasoning the previous roster used for this role.

wild_croaker._comment: GREEN ON GREEN, FIXED. Ships #80a960, which is the meadow's own hue. Now a saturated water blue at hue 199° with a gold belly for internal value contrast — and a Water creature that is water-coloured says its type before any UI does.

wild_stalker._comment: Crimson rather than the pack's fox-orange #b67343, which sat inside the starter's amber. An aggressive skulker gets the one hue in the roster that is nothing but a warning.

wild_pup._comment: The young half of the one evolution line. Pale lilac at value 0.71 — the Gloamfang's indigo, lightened and drained, with the same amber eye. Evolution should read in the palette and not only in the table.

evolved_wolf._comment: PALE GREY ON GREY, FIXED. Ships #777972 at saturation 0.03 and the ground's value. Now a deep indigo at hue 231° — hue-opposed to a green world — carrying a near-white cold ruff so the creature has strong value contrast inside its own silhouette, and amber eyes, which are the cheapest menace available and the through-line to the Duskpup.

wild_bristler._comment: The ambusher, and the first creature in this project bigger than the trainer. Dark warm umber so a heavy mass holds against grass, with the only two bright marks on the body at the end that hurts you: bone horns and amber eyes.

wild_grazer._comment:
The mount, and the tallest thing in the meadow. Near-white against olive is the largest value separation on offer and no other creature is anywhere near it. Warm ivory rather than pure white — MA-05 called an untextured near-white ruin out for reading unlit — with bone antlers and a dark muzzle and hooves so the silhouette does not dissolve into one flat shape.

The pack names these zones `Material`, `Material.001` and so on, which is why this map is keyed by species and not globally: the Husky uses `Material.001` for black fur. Which zone is which was read off the RENDER and corrected — the first pass assumed `Material.010` was the antlers because it was the mid-brown, and the antlers came out slate grey.
